sandhi.note: Visarga before c becomes s, and s next to c becomes ś (क्षीरोदश्च); then a + a → ā (चामलं). The final m of अमलम् is anusvāra before the h of हारम् (मोऽनुस्वारः, 8.3.23).

sandhi.rule: मोऽनुस्वारः (8.3.23) does not apply before a vowel
sandhi.note: Final m stays m before a vowel and is written together with it.

samasa.sense: the Ocean of Milk, personified as a giver
samasa.alt: Also analysed as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, क्षीरस्य उदः ‘the water of milk’, i.e. the milk-sea; the bahuvrīhi suits a personified giver. उद stands for उदक as the final member of such compounds.

samasa.sense: a jewel worn on the crown of the head
samasa.alt: Also saptamī tatpuruṣa, चूडायां मणिः ‘the jewel (worn) on the crest’; the sense is the same.

morph.note: Neuter dual of an a-stem (nom./acc. -e): ‘two garments’, the upper and the lower cloth. With अजरे it is a pair of everlasting robes.
Neuter dual again: earrings come as a pair, so the dual is the natural number. A dual in -e is pragṛhya, but here both duals stand before consonants, so no hiatus arises.

mantras.anvaya: क्षीरोदः च अमलं हारम्, अजरे अम्बरे च, तथा दिव्यं चूडामणिम्, कुण्डले कटकानि च (ददौ)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The verse has a subject and a string of objects but no verb of its own; ददौ, the verb of the whole catalogue (2.20–31), is supplied. The list of ornaments runs on into 2.26 and 2.27a.
mantras.lit: And the Milk-Ocean (gave) a spotless necklace and likewise two unaging garments, likewise a divine crest-jewel, two earrings and bracelets,
mantras.tr: The Ocean of Milk gave her a spotless necklace, a pair of garments that never wear out, a heavenly crest-jewel, earrings and bracelets,
mantras.tr_note: ‘Gave her’ is supplied from the catalogue’s verb ददौ; the sentence continues into 2.26–27.

comm.t: After the weapons come the ornaments. The Ocean of Milk, the store of treasures in Purāṇic myth, dresses the newly formed Goddess: necklace, a pair of imperishable garments, crest-jewel, earrings and bracelets. The verse names a giver but no verb; the list continues for a verse and a half.

Where the list of the Ocean’s gifts ends is not marked. The usual reading lets it run to the finger-rings of 2.27a, so that Viśvakarman’s gift begins with the axe; others give the jewellery after the garments to the craftsman Viśvakarman, whose verb ददौ follows in 2.27. The Sanskrit allows both.

flags.uncertain: The verse has no verb, and the boundary between the Ocean’s gifts and Viśvakarman’s (2.27) is not marked in the text; the translation follows the common reading (the Ocean gives everything to the rings of 2.27a).

samasa.type: tatpuruṣa (ekadeśin type: the part named first, ‘half of the moon’)
samasa.sense: a crescent-shaped ornament, worn on the head or brow
samasa.alt: Also taken as a karmadhāraya, अर्धः चासौ चन्द्रः च ‘a half moon’; the meaning is the same.

samasa.vigraha: सर्वे च ते बाहवः च, तेषु
samasa.sense: on every one of her many arms

samasa.literal: that than which there is no higher

morph.note: The taddhita -vat of comparison added to तद्: ‘like that, likewise’. It is an indeclinable and must not be confused with the possessive -vat of हिमवत् (2.29).
Masculine dual (-au): anklets, like earrings, are named as a pair.

mantras.anvaya: तथा शुभ्रम् अर्धचन्द्रम्, सर्वबाहुषु केयूरान्, तद्वत् विमलौ नूपुरौ, अनुत्तमं ग्रैवेयकं (च ददौ)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A continuation of the list begun in 2.25, all accusatives of the supplied verb; सर्वबाहुषु says where the armlets are worn.
mantras.lit: likewise a bright half-moon, armlets on all the arms, likewise two spotless anklets, an unsurpassed neck-ornament,
mantras.tr: a gleaming crescent, armlets for all her arms, a pair of shining anklets and a peerless collar,
mantras.tr_note: The sentence continues from 2.25 and into 2.27.

comm.t: The list of ornaments continues from head to foot: a crescent for the head, armlets for ‘all her arms’, anklets and a collar. The plural arms anticipate 2.39, where she fills the directions with a thousand arms.

The same ornament vocabulary describes the Goddess’s form in the Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa): 31, कनकाङ्गदकेयूरकमनीयभुजान्विता (arms lovely with golden aṅgadas and keyūras), and 32, रत्नग्रैवेयचिन्ताकलोलमुक्ताफलान्विता (with a jewelled graiveya and pearls). This is a shared iconographic vocabulary, not a borrowing between the two texts.

samasa.sense: the finest rings (रत्न at the end of a compound means ‘the best of its kind’)
samasa.alt: Also read as ‘gem-rings’, रत्नमयानि अङ्गुलीयकानि, a madhyamapadalopin karmadhāraya with the members reversed; but the head of the compound is रत्न, which favours ‘the jewels among rings’.

samasa.sense: the maker of all things, the divine artisan

samasa.type: tatpuruṣa (prādi); निर्मल is itself a bahuvrīhi, निर्गतः मलः यस्मात् तत्

morph.note: Perfect of √दा: reduplicated दद- with the ending -au that roots in -ā take in the 1st and 3rd singular perfect (ददौ ‘he gave’). The catalogue’s refrain verb.
Nominative singular of an n-stem: the final n is dropped and the vowel lengthened (कर्मन् → कर्मा), as in राजा.

mantras.anvaya: समस्तासु अङ्गुलीषु अङ्गुलीयकरत्नानि च (क्षीरोदः ददौ)। विश्वकर्मा तस्यै अतिनिर्मलं परशुं च (अनेकरूपाणि अस्त्राणि अभेद्यं दंशनं च) ददौ।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line ends the Ocean’s list (2.25–26); the second begins a new giver, Viśvakarman, whose objects continue into the first line of 2.28.
mantras.lit: and jewel-rings on all the fingers. Viśvakarman gave to her an exceedingly spotless axe and
mantras.tr: and the finest rings for every finger. Viśvakarman gave her a gleaming axe,
mantras.tr_note: The first line is taken as the last of the Ocean’s gifts (see 2.25); the second line runs on into 2.28.

comm.t: Rings for every finger complete the jewellery. Viśvakarman, the craftsman of the gods, gives the axe and, in the next line, missiles and armour.

The axe (परशु) appears in the madhyama-carita dhyāna (Gita Press pāṭha), where Mahālakṣmī holds अक्षस्रक्परशुं … — rosary and axe are the first two objects named. The dhyāna gathers the gifts of this chapter into eighteen hands.

bahuvrīhi; अम्लान is a nañ tatpuruṣa (न म्लानम्, √म्लै + kta) and पङ्कज an upapada tatpuruṣa (पङ्के जायते इति)
samasa.sense: a garland of lotuses that never fade

morph.note: Gerundive (ṇyat) of √भिद् with the negative prefix: ‘not to be split’ — the armour cannot be pierced.
Locative of the s-stem शिरस्, like उरसि from उरस्: the locative tells where each garland is to be worn.

mantras.anvaya: (विश्वकर्मा) अनेकरूपाणि अस्त्राणि तथा अभेद्यं दंशनं च (ददौ)। (जलधिः) शिरसि अम्लानपङ्कजां मालाम्, उरसि च अपरां (मालाम्, अददत्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes Viśvakarman’s gift (verb ददौ in 2.27); the second line lists objects of अददत्, whose subject जलधिः stands in 2.29.
mantras.lit: missiles of many forms, and likewise an impenetrable armour; a garland of unfading lotuses for the head, and another for the breast —
mantras.tr: missiles of many kinds and armour that nothing can pierce. A garland of unfading lotuses for her head and another for her breast
mantras.tr_note: The second line is the object of ‘the Ocean gave’ in 2.29; the translation leaves the verb to that verse.

comm.t: Viśvakarman’s gifts end with missiles and impenetrable armour. The garlands — one for the head, one for the breast — belong to the next giver, the Ocean, named in 2.29.

Unfading lotuses (अम्लान) are a stock sign of the divine: what the gods wear does not wither. The lotus also stands in the madhyama-carita dhyāna (पद्मं), and she is pictured there as seated on a lotus (सरोजस्थिताम्).

sandhi.note: Final t before j becomes j (t voiced to d, and the dental made palatal next to the palatal j): अददज्जलधिः. Then the visarga before t becomes s: जलधिस्तस्यै.

sandhi.rule: मोऽनुस्वारः (8.3.23) for वाहनं; final n before v is unchanged
sandhi.note: Final n before v stays n; only the m of वाहनम् becomes anusvāra before s (मोऽनुस्वारः, 8.3.23).

morph.note: Imperfect of √दा. Classical grammar has अददात् (reduplicated stem ददा-); the epics often inflect √दा on a thematic stem दद-, giving अददत्. The metre (eight syllables, अ-द-दज्-ज-ल-धिस्-तस्-यै) is unaffected either way, so this is a matter of usage, not of metre.
Nominative singular of the possessive -vat stem हिमवत्: the vowel is lengthened and n inserted (-वान्), as in भगवान्.

mantras.anvaya: जलधिः तस्यै (शिरसि अम्लानपङ्कजां मालाम्, उरसि च अपराम्,) अतिशोभनं पङ्कजं च अददत्। हिमवान् वाहनं सिंहं विविधानि रत्नानि च (ददौ)।
mantras.anvaya_en: अददत् governs the garlands of 2.28b and the lotus; Himavat’s verb is supplied. वाहनम् is predicative: ‘a lion as her mount’.
mantras.lit: the Ocean gave to her, and an exceedingly beautiful lotus. Himavat (gave) a lion as mount, and various jewels.
mantras.tr: the Ocean gave her, with a lotus of surpassing beauty. Himavat gave her a lion to ride, and jewels of every kind.

comm.t: The Ocean (जलधि, distinct from the Ocean of Milk of 2.25) gives garlands and a lotus. Himavat gives the lion that will carry her and fight beside her (2.51; it battles Cāmara in 3.14–16).
Himavat is, in Purāṇic tradition, the father of Pārvatī; here the mountain simply gives what belongs to the mountains — the lion and its jewels. The lion-mount gives her the name सिंहवाहिनी in 2.34.
